statement: A real-valued square matrix $Q$ of size $n \times n$ is an orthogonal matrix (or orthonormal matrix) if its columns and rows form an orthonormal basis of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the ordinary Euclidean dot product, satisfying $Q^{\mathrm{T}}Q = QQ^{\mathrm{T}} = I$, or equivalently $Q^{-1} = Q^{\mathrm{T}}$.

symbols.meaning: dimension of the Euclidean space and matrix order

properties.property: The determinant of any orthogonal matrix is +1 or -1 (\det(Q) = \pm 1).
An orthogonal matrix is invertible, and its inverse equals its transpose (Q^{-1} = Q^{\mathrm{T}}), which is also an orthogonal matrix.
properties.why: Direct consequence of Q^{\mathrm{T}}Q = I and the group properties under matrix inversion

properties.property: All eigenvalues of an orthogonal matrix have complex modulus 1.
properties.why: Any orthogonal matrix can be diagonalized over the complex numbers into 2 x 2 rotation blocks and \pm 1 real entries lying on the unit circle

properties.property: The set of all n x n orthogonal matrices forms a compact Lie group O(n) of dimension n(n - 1)/2.
properties.why: Matrix multiplication and inversion preserve orthogonality, and SO(n) has (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2 degrees of freedom

properties.property: The condition number of an orthogonal matrix is 1 (the minimum possible), preserving numerical stability.
properties.why: Having determinant \pm 1 and all eigenvalues of magnitude 1 prevents magnification of errors under multiplication

properties.property: The Lie algebra of the orthogonal matrix group consists of skew-symmetric matrices (\dot{Q}^{\mathrm{T}} = -\dot{Q}).
properties.why: Differentiating Q^{\mathrm{T}}Q = I at t = 0 (where Q = I) yields \dot{Q}^{\mathrm{T}}Q + Q^{\mathrm{T}}\dot{Q} = 0

assumptions.assumption: The matrix Q is square and real-valued.
assumptions.breaks_when: The matrix is rectangular (m != n) or complex-valued (where unitary matrices U*U = I apply).

assumptions.assumption: Orthonormality of vectors is defined under the standard Euclidean dot product on R^n.
assumptions.breaks_when: The space is equipped with an indefinite or non-standard metric tensor.

failure_modes.mode: Confusing orthogonal columns with an orthogonal matrix
failure_modes.signature: M^{\mathrm{T}}M = D where D is a diagonal matrix with D != I
failure_modes.cause: The columns of the matrix are mutually orthogonal but not normalized to unit length.
Having determinant +/-1 is a necessary consequence of orthogonality but not a sufficient condition (e.g., diag(2, 1/2)).
